nameStory: The "sand" in sand catchfly comes from this plant's love of sandy soils and dunes where it makes its home. The "catchfly" name refers to the sticky stems that can trap small insects - though unlike some of its relatives, this species isn't particularly sticky compared to other catchflies in the Silene family.
description: Sand catchfly is a small annual wildflower that grows in sandy places throughout Europe and western Asia, with very rare appearances in New England. This delicate plant produces bright pink flowers with distinctive parallel veins running down the inflated flower base (called a calyx). It's a low-growing plant that completes its entire life cycle in one growing season, making it easy to miss if you're not looking at the right time.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink petals emerge from an inflated, balloon-like base with prominent parallel veins running lengthwise - these veins look like pinstripes on the rounded flower base

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that stays close to the ground, with a delicate, somewhat sprawling appearance typical of plants adapted to sandy conditions

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Exclusively found in sandy soils, dunes, and other well-drained sandy areas where few other wildflowers can establish

idTips.label: Stem Texture
idTips.description: Stems have a slightly sticky feel when touched, though less dramatically sticky than many other catchfly species

habitat: In New England, sand catchfly would be found in coastal dunes, sandy beaches, or other areas with very well-drained sandy soils. It prefers open, sunny locations where the sandy substrate doesn't retain much moisture, making it quite specialized in its habitat requirements.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, and young plants begin establishing their low-growing rosettes in sandy areas.
seasonality.summer: Bright pink flowers bloom during the warmest months, displaying their characteristic striped, inflated bases. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Plants complete their annual cycle by setting seed and dying back, leaving seeds to overwinter in the sandy soil.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts visible - exists only as seeds waiting in the sand for spring warmth to trigger germination.

funFact: Sand catchfly has the largest mitochondrial genome ever discovered in any organism - a whopping 11.3 million base pairs, which is about 275 times larger than a typical plant's mitochondrial DNA and even larger than some entire bacterial genomes!
confusionNotes: The bright pink petals and distinctively striped, balloon-like flower base make sand catchfly quite unique among New England wildflowers. The parallel veins on the inflated calyx are the key feature - no other pink wildflower in our region has this pinstriped balloon appearance.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, sand catchfly is extremely rare in our region and may represent a casual introduction rather than an established population. Most North American field guides focus on the more common native catchflies, so this European species might not appear in regional wildflower books.
compareHints: Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out. The parallel-veined, inflated calyx is much more pronounced than in sleepy catchfly or wild pink, and the sandy habitat preference distinguishes it from woodland species like fire pink or starry campion.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
